paper_metadata.title: Solid-state poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) nanofoams. Part I: Low-temperature CO2 sorption, diffusion, and the depression in PMMA glass transition
paper_metadata.source_filename: Solid-state poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) nanofoams. Part I- Low-temperature CO2 sorption, diffusion, and the depression in PMMA glass transition.pdf

SYNTH.question: What are the number-average (Mn) and weight-average (Mw) molecular weights of the PMMA used in this study?
Under what pressure and temperature conditions was the maximum reported CO2 solubility of 39.3 wt% achieved in PMMA?
SYNTH.expected_answer: A saturation pressure of 5 MPa and a saturation temperature of -30 °C.

SYNTH.question: How does the incorporation of 39.3% CO2 affect the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PMMA?
SYNTH.expected_answer: It decreases the Tg from 103 °C to -12.5 °C.

SYNTH.question: Why is PMMA considered to have very high CO2 solubility compared to other polymers under similar conditions?
SYNTH.expected_answer: It is probably due to the high mass density of carbonyl groups in PMMA.

SYNTH.question: How does the saturation temperature affect the sorption diffusivity of CO2 in PMMA?
SYNTH.expected_answer: Temperature has a profound effect; diffusivity increases with temperature, ranging from 2.5 x 10^-8 cm2/s at -30 °C to 3.65 x 10^-7 cm2/s at 10 °C.

SYNTH.question: Under what saturation pressure and temperature range was the CO2 sorption process carried out for the PMMA samples?
SYNTH.expected_answer: The saturation pressure was fixed at 5 MPa and the saturation temperature (T sat) varied from -30 °C to 100 °C.

SYNTH.question: How does the incorporation of CO2 into PMMA affect the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the polymer?
SYNTH.expected_answer: The dissolution of CO2 plasticizes the polymer, lowering its glass transition temperature; specifically, the incorporation of 39.3% CO2 decreases the Tg from 103 °C to -12.5 °C.

CHAR.question: Which method was used to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 system, and what specific visual criteria were used to identify the minimum foaming temperature?
CHAR.expected_answer: The minimum foaming temperature approach was used. The Tg was identified as the average of two adjacent foaming temperatures where the sample remains transparent at the lower temperature and becomes opaque (indicating bubble formation) at the higher temperature.
CHAR.revise_reason: The original question asked for DSC details which are not in the text; the revised question asks for the actual method (minimum foaming temperature) and criteria (transparency vs. opacity) explicitly described in the evidence.

CHAR.question: What were the reported weight-average molecular weight (Mw) and number-average molecular weight (Mn) for the PMMA used in this study?
CHAR.revise_reason: The evidence passages describe solubility, diffusivity, and Tg depression but do not list the molecular weight (Mn/Mw) of the starting PMMA material, making it impossible to answer based strictly on the provided text.

CHAR.question: How was the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 mixture determined experimentally?
CHAR.expected_answer: It was determined by a minimum foaming temperature approach, where the average value of two adjacent foaming temperatures (one where the sample remains transparent and one where it becomes opaque) was used, with SEM images used to confirm cell formation.

CHAR.question: What is the reported solubility of CO2 in PMMA at a saturation temperature of -30 °C and a pressure of 5 MPa?
What is the activation energy for diffusion (DHD) of CO2 in PMMA in region 1?
How was the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 system determined in this study, and what equipment was used to control the foaming temperature?
CHAR.expected_answer: Tg was determined using the minimum foaming temperature approach, where samples were immersed in a silicone oil bath (Thermo Haake B5) set at specific foaming temperatures; the Tg was taken as the average of the temperatures where the sample transitions from transparent to opaque.
CHAR.revise_reason: The original question incorrectly assumed a DSC measurement; the revised question accurately reflects the 'minimum foaming temperature' method and the specific equipment (silicone oil bath) mentioned in the text.

CHAR.question: What are the activation energies (DHD) for CO2 diffusion in PMMA for the four identified diffusion regions?
CHAR.expected_answer: The activation energies are 22.8 kJ/mol for Region 1, -12.6 kJ/mol for Region 2, -57.6 kJ/mol for Region 3, and 39.8 kJ/mol for Region 4.

PROC.question: What saturation pressure and temperature range were used to determine the CO2 solubility in PMMA?
PROC.expected_answer: The saturation pressure was fixed at 5 MPa, and the saturation temperature (T sat) varied from -30 °C to 100 °C.

PROC.question: How does the amount of absorbed CO2 affect the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PMMA?
PROC.expected_answer: The absorption of CO2 plasticizes the polymer and reduces the Tg; specifically, it decreases from 103 °C to -12.5 °C when 39.3% CO2 is incorporated, averaging a 3 °C reduction for every 1% increase in CO2 absorbed.

PROC.question: Why was a saturation pressure of 5 MPa selected for the CO2 sorption experiments in PMMA?
PROC.expected_answer: 5 MPa was chosen to maximize CO2 sorption in the polymer while eliminating the need for a pressure boosting device, as it is slightly below the pressure of a full CO2 gas cylinder at room temperature.

PROC.question: How does the relationship between saturation temperature (Tsat) and glass transition temperature (Tg) determine the physical state of the PMMA-CO2 mixture?
PROC.expected_answer: The system is in a rubbery state when the saturation temperature is greater than the glass transition temperature (Tsat > Tg), and it is in a glassy state when the saturation temperature is below the glass transition temperature (Tsat < Tg).

PROC.question: What method was used to determine the minimum foaming temperature of the PMMA-CO2 system?
PROC.expected_answer: Saturated samples were immersed in a silicone oil bath at foaming temperatures (Tf) ranging from -20 °C to 120 °C in 5 °C intervals; the minimum foaming temperature was identified as the average of the two adjacent temperatures where the sample transitioned from transparent (no foaming) to opaque (bubble formation).

PROC.question: How does decreasing the saturation temperature from 100 °C to -30 °C affect the solubility of CO2 in PMMA?
PROC.expected_answer: The solubility of CO2 in PMMA increases ten-fold, from 3.9% at 100 °C to 39.3% at -30 °C.

PROC.question: Why was a low-temperature CO2 saturation process explored for the production of PMMA nanofoams?
PROC.expected_answer: It was explored to determine if the higher gas solubility achieved at lower saturation temperatures could be used in a solid-state process to reduce the cell size from the order of 100 nm to the order of 10 nm.

COMP.question: Which empirical and theoretical models were used to predict the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 mixture?
COMP.expected_answer: The Fox equation, Jenckel & Heusch (J&H) equation, Gordon & Taylor (G&T) equation, and Chow's model.

COMP.question: How does the equilibrium mass percentage of CO2 absorbed into PMMA affect its glass transition temperature (Tg)?
COMP.expected_answer: The Tg decreases as the mass% of CO2 increases; specifically, it reduces from 103 °C to -12.5 °C when CO2 absorption increases to 39.3%, averaging a 3 °C reduction per 1% increase in CO2.

COMP.question: What specific parameters were used for the implementation of Chow's model to predict the Tg of the PMMA-CO2 system?
COMP.expected_answer: The lattice coordination number z = 2 and the excess transition isobaric specific heat of the polymer DCpp = 0.265 J K-1 g-1.

COMP.question: How does the predictive performance of Chow's model compare to the experimental Tg data for the PMMA-CO2 system?
COMP.expected_answer: Chow's model predicts the general decreasing trend of Tg but performs poorly in absolute values, consistently underestimating the Tg compared to experimental data.

COMP.question: What is the relationship between saturation temperature (Tsat) and the solubility of CO2 in PMMA?
COMP.expected_answer: Solubility increases as saturation temperature decreases, showing a ten-fold increase from 3.9% at 100 °C to 39.3% at -30 °C, and can be described with an Arrhenius relationship.

COMP.question: What are the specific activation energy values for CO2 diffusion in PMMA across the four identified diffusion regions?
COMP.expected_answer: The specific activation energy values for each region are not provided in the text; however, the text identifies four distinct regions where diffusivity varies differently with temperature, characterized by different activation energies, with negative activation energy observed in regions 2 and 3.
COMP.revise_reason: The original question and expected answer contained hallucinated numerical values for activation energies that are not present in the evidence; the revision corrects the question to ask for the existence of these values and updates the answer to reflect that the specific numbers are not reported, only the qualitative behavior and region definitions.

COMP.question: Which empirical models were used to fit the experimental data for the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 mixture?
COMP.expected_answer: The Fox equation, Jenckel & Heusche equation, Gordon & Taylor equation, and Chow's model.

ONTO.expected_answer: A subclass of Method or Model (specifically a mathematical model used to characterize a property).

STU.question: What is the glass transition temperature (Tg) of neat PMMA?
STU.expected_answer: The glass transition temperature (Tg) of neat PMMA was measured to be 103 °C.

STU.question: Which method was used to determine the glass transition temperature of the PMMA-CO2 mixture?
STU.expected_answer: The glass transition temperature was determined by a minimum foaming temperature approach.

STU.question: Why was a saturation pressure of 5 MPa chosen for the CO2 sorption experiments?
STU.expected_answer: 5 MPa was chosen to maximize CO2 sorption in the polymer and eliminate the need for a pressure boosting device, as it is slightly below the pressure of a full CO2 gas cylinder at room temperature.

STU.question: What is the relationship between the saturation temperature and the solubility of CO2 in PMMA?
STU.expected_answer: Solubility increases as the saturation temperature decreases; for example, it increases ten-fold from 3.9% at 100 °C to 39.3% at -30 °C.

STU.question: Which method was used to determine the diffusivity of CO2 from the sorption plots?
STU.expected_answer: The hybrid method was used to determine diffusivity because it is more accurate, fitting data from the whole sorption curve including both short-time and long-time data.

STU.question: Why was low-temperature CO2 saturation explored as a method for producing PMMA nanofoams?
STU.expected_answer: Low-temperature CO2 saturation was explored because gas solubility in polymers generally increases as the saturation temperature decreases, and a higher amount of absorbed gas leads to a higher number of cells to nucleate, which can drive down the cell size from the order of 100 nm to 10 nm.

STU.question: By which process were the PMMA nanofoams with 30-40 nm cells produced?
STU.expected_answer: The PMMA nanofoams with 30-40 nm cells were produced using a solid-state foaming process based on low-temperature CO2 saturation.

PHD.question: What limitation is acknowledged regarding the predictive accuracy of Chow's model for the glass transition temperature of the PMMA-CO2 system?
PHD.expected_answer: Chow's model predicts the general decreasing trend of Tg, but it predicts the values poorly, with the predictions always being lower than the experimental data.

PHD.question: How does the maximum CO2 solubility reported in this study compare to previously reported values for PMMA?
PHD.expected_answer: The study reports a solubility of 39.3% at -30 °C, which the authors state is the highest amount of CO2 ever reported absorbed in PMMA.

PHD.question: How does the change in the heat of sorption (DHs) around the CO2 vaporization temperature affect the solubility of CO2 in PMMA at very low temperatures?
PHD.expected_answer: The drop in DHs leads to a slower increase in solubility with decreasing temperature; without this change, the solubility at -30 °C would have been approximately 70% instead of the measured 39.3%.

PHD.question: Why was a saturation pressure of 5 MPa selected for the sorption experiments?
PHD.expected_answer: 5 MPa was chosen to maximize CO2 sorption in the polymer while eliminating the need for a pressure boosting device, as it is slightly below the pressure of a full CO2 gas cylinder at room temperature.

PHD.question: What remains unknown regarding the physical mechanism of the negative activation energy of diffusion observed in the PMMA-CO2 system?
PHD.expected_answer: The authors state that the physical mechanism for the negative activation energy of diffusion in the PMMA-CO2 system is currently under investigation, as mechanisms proposed for other systems (like Ag in Ni or pHEMA-based hydrogels) are not applicable.

PHD.question: Why was low-temperature CO2 saturation selected as the primary mechanism to reduce the cell size of PMMA nanofoams compared to traditional high-pressure methods?
PHD.expected_answer: Low-temperature CO2 saturation was used because gas solubility in polymers generally increases as the saturation temperature decreases; higher gas solubility leads to a higher number of cells nucleating in a unit volume, which can drive the cell size down from the order of 100 nm to the order of 10 nm.

PHD.question: What limitation does the paper acknowledge regarding the current understanding of the physical mechanism for negative activation energy of diffusion in the PMMA-CO2 system?
PHD.expected_answer: The paper acknowledges that the physical mechanism for negative activation energy of diffusion in the PMMA-CO2 system is currently under investigation, as previously proposed mechanisms for other systems (such as complex defects in Ag-Ni or temperature-dependent swelling in pHEMA-based hydrogels) are not applicable to this polymer-gas system.

CHAR.question: Which method was used to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the PMMA-CO2 system, and what specific visual criteria were used to identify the minimum foaming temperature?
CHAR.expected_answer: The minimum foaming temperature approach was used. The Tg was identified as the average of two adjacent foaming temperatures where the sample remains transparent at the lower temperature and becomes opaque (indicating bubble formation) at the higher temperature.
CHAR.revise_reason: The original question asked for DSC details which are not in the text; the revised question asks for the actual method (minimum foaming temperature) and criteria (transparency vs. opacity) explicitly described in the evidence.

CHAR.expected_answer: Tg was determined using the minimum foaming temperature approach, where samples were immersed in a silicone oil bath (Thermo Haake B5) set at specific foaming temperatures; the Tg was taken as the average of the temperatures where the sample transitions from transparent to opaque.
CHAR.revise_reason: The original question incorrectly assumed a DSC measurement; the revised question accurately reflects the 'minimum foaming temperature' method and the specific equipment (silicone oil bath) mentioned in the text.

models._note: Three distinct LLM families (Qwen / Gemma / DeepSeek) across stages for cross-family diversity. Embeddings via LOCAL sentence-transformers (deterministic, no network) because the shared Ollama bge-m3 endpoint is unreliable from inside long-running pipeline processes (see history v1.3). All LLM calls use think=false + format=json on the client.
_history: v0: cq_generator=llama4:scout -> failed to produce JSON output; switched to qwen3:32b + format=json.
v0.5: all stages on qwen3:32b/deepseek-r1:32b; embedder local BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5.
v1.0: per-stage model selection, bge-m3 via Ollama, refiner added, evaluator reduced to 5 reference-free families.

v1.1: reverted embedder to local BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 because the shared Ollama bge-m3 endpoint was returning 500s. Added per-question evidence retrieval in validator + refiner to fix a truncation bug (was capping evidence at 7000 chars regardless of how many passages were available).

v1.2: switched embedder back to bge-m3 via Ollama after a probe showed the endpoint was responsive when called with proper exponential-backoff retry. Added 1s process-wide throttling between embed calls.

v1.3 (this version): reverted to local BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5. The bge-m3 Ollama path stays healthy in isolation (standalone curl + Python) but the long-running pipeline process gets sustained 500s in stages 5-6, even with exponential backoff, 1s throttling, AND Connection: close to force fresh TCP per call. Most likely cause is the shared upstream evicting bge-m3 from memory while the heavy LLMs (gemma4:31b, deepseek-r1:32b) are loaded, with the eviction window outlasting our 230s retry budget. Local sentence-transformers is slightly lower quality (384-dim vs 1024) but always finishes.
